meta.regime: The regime is a pure supply shock priced through a rate-differential market, and the two words that matter are what it is NOT. It is not a risk-off shock: on a day when the main Hormuz bypass pipeline stayed shut, diplomacy collapsed and a tanker burned, gold FELL 0.50%, silver fell 0.67% and the Swiss franc lost 0.26% to the dollar. Havens are not being bought. It is not a demand shock either: the IEA cut its 2026 global demand forecast to a DECLINE of 2.5 million barrels a day, steeper than August's 1.6 million, and OPEC cut its demand-growth forecast for a fifth straight month - yet crude rose 2% anyway, because the barrels physically cannot move. What that leaves is a market where energy prices are set by pipes and straits while currencies are set by policy differentials, and the two channels only intersect in one place: the terms of trade. That is why CAD outperformed today and why the euro area, the largest net energy importer on this board with German gas at 80.65 euros a megawatt-hour and up 29.32% on the month, underperformed. The fourth feature is calendar compression - the Fed, the Bank of England and the Bank of Japan all decide inside 61 hours - which means every symbol on this board is effectively a bet on how those three land relative to what is already priced, with roughly 86% priced on the Fed and near-certainty priced on the BoJ.
meta.nextBigEvent: FOMC decision plus the Summary of Economic Projections, Wednesday September 16 at 18:00Z, press conference 18:30Z. TE carries consensus AND its own forecast at 4.00%, and CME FedWatch sits near 86%, up from 72% before last week's PPI. The hike is not the event - it is bought. The event is the dot plot, because TE's projection rows still show 3.6% for the first year and 3.4% for the second against 3.8% for the current year, which is a set of dots that implies CUTS after this hike. If Warsh's committee lifts those out-year dots to flat or higher, the dollar finally gets the trend that an 86% hike probability and a 4.9%-handle 10-year have not delivered all month; if the dots keep the easing path intact, the market reads Wednesday as the last hike and sells the fact. Warsh has refused forward guidance since Jackson Hole on August 28, so the dots are the only guidance available and their weight is unusually high. Before that, Canada CPI lands today at 12:30Z with the monthly rate expected to fall to 0.0% from +0.5%.

dailyRead: Start with the fact that did not move a score but should change how the whole board is read. Over the weekend two doors closed at once. Saudi Arabia's East-West pipeline - Petroline, 1,200 kilometres from the Eastern Province to the Red Sea port of Yanbu, carrying roughly 5 million barrels a day of crude that would otherwise transit the Gulf - was hit by drones launched from Iraq on September 10 and 11 and remains shut. Traders told Reuters that stored volumes at Yanbu cover exports for only five to seven days; past that window as much as 4% of global oil supply is exposed. Then, late Sunday, Omani Foreign Minister Badr Albusaidi announced that Monday's Gulf Cooperation Council-Iran meeting on the Strait of Hormuz shipping proposal had been postponed 'in the interests of consensus', at the request of unnamed regional states and by joint Tehran-Muscat decision, with no new date set. That announcement came hours after a vessel was struck near Qeshm Island killing one and injuring four, with Trump declining to say whether the US was responsible. So: the bypass is closed, the strait is still roughly 90% below pre-war flows, and the diplomatic track has no date on the calendar. Crude did exactly what it should: WTI +2.17% to 102.226, Brent +2.09% to 106.795, EU gas +4.30% to 82.94 euros. And here is the part that matters for FX. GOLD FELL. XAU/USD is at 4328.57, down 0.50% on the day, down 1.73% on the week and down 1.98% on the month. Silver fell 0.67% to 63.834. The Swiss franc lost another 0.26%, taking USD/CHF to 0.81862, up 1.12% on the week. Yesterday this file cut CHF from +1 to zero on the argument that a haven which will not bid on a burning tanker cannot be held long. Twenty-four hours later that call is validated by a completely independent asset: gold, with no central bank and no intervention risk attached to it, refused the same escalation. This is not a risk-off market. It is a market in which US real rates dominate everything and the war is being expressed exclusively through the price of physical energy. Second point, and this one IS a change: the petro-currency link came back. Yesterday's file said plainly that Brent gaining 9% on the week while USD/CAD rose 0.25% meant USOIL LONG and CAD LONG were no longer the same trade. Today they are the same trade again. USD/CAD sits at 1.38770, up just 0.03%, on a session in which the dollar index rose 0.32% to 99.439 and beat every other major - EUR -0.39%, NZD -0.53%, EUR/USD to 1.15535, NZD/USD to 0.57823. The Canadian dollar was the best G10 performer of the day. The specific fact that changed is the character of the oil move: last week's 9% was a risk premium, and risk premia do not transmit to a petro-currency when the domestic central bank is frozen. A pipeline that is physically shut with a five-to-seven-day inventory buffer is a supply shock, and supply shocks move the terms of trade directly. CAD is not upgraded, and the reason is discipline rather than doubt: Canada's own August CPI prints at 12:30Z today with the monthly rate expected to collapse to 0.0% from +0.5%, trimmed-mean at 1.9% and median at 2.0%, and August employment was -41,700 with retail sales -0.8% m/m. Core measures at or below target keep the Bank of Canada frozen no matter where crude trades, and raising a score hours before its own inflation print on one session of price action is exactly the noise-chasing this file is supposed to avoid. If today's CPI does not disappoint, CAD is the first upgrade candidate on the board. Third, and this needs saying straight because yesterday's argument depended on it: the yen did NOT beat the dollar today. USD/JPY rose 0.37% to 154.177 and the weekly loss has shrunk to -0.12% from -1.69% at Friday's close; the monthly is still -3.31%. Yesterday JPY was held at +3 specifically because it won the head-to-head on the hottest US data day of the month. That evidence did not repeat. JPY still holds +3, but the honest description is that the score is now a FORWARD call rather than a validated result: the BoJ is expected to move to 1.25% on Friday, the highest policy rate since roughly 1995, DBS calls it 'almost a done deal' with a hawkish 25bp the most likely outcome, and 62% of surveyed economists see 1.75% by end-Q2 2027. One 0.37% session inside a broad dollar bid is not a reason to flip a +3, but it is a reason to name the invalidation precisely: a hike delivered Friday with an explicit pause attached is the single event that cuts the yen and unwinds every SHORT XXX/JPY on this list at once. Fourth, the base rates. Nothing printed overnight in the eight economies. TE was re-verified this morning across all of them and every value matches yesterday: US CPI 3.4% with the policy rate at a 3.75% upper bound and FedWatch near 86%; euro-area HICP 3.3% with the ECB deposit facility confirmed at 2.50% after the September 10 hike from 2.25%, main refinancing 2.65%, marginal lending 2.90%; UK CPI 2.9% and Bank Rate 3.75%; Japan CPI 1.9% and the policy rate 1.00%; Australia CPI 3.5% and the cash rate 4.35%; New Zealand CPI 4.1% and the OCR 2.75%; Canada CPI 3.0% and the overnight rate 2.25%; Switzerland CPI 0.8% and the SNB at exactly 0%. Fifth, the industrial complex is deteriorating faster than anything else on this board and it is the AUD tripwire. Copper is at 6.3838 USD per pound, down 1.32% today, down 5.27% on the WEEK and down 3.33% on the month - a materially worse reading than the -1.42% monthly figure that framed Thursday's discussion. Yesterday's file set a two-part trigger for cutting Australia to zero, copper plus domestic employment, and said the employment half could not be tested until the mid-October labour force report. That rule is kept today, so AUD holds +1, but it is now the weakest +1 on the board and the test arrives sooner than October: China industrial production and retail sales print Tuesday at 05:00Z with consensus at 4.8% and 0.8%. A miss on both, with copper already down 5% in five sessions, meets the spirit of the trigger through the demand channel rather than the domestic one, and AUD goes to zero. Consumer confidence at 84.4 from 88.9 and building permits at 17,687 from 18,351 are already pointing the same way. Sixth, sterling. GBP stays at zero because both tails are live inside 48 hours and the calendar loads them in the worst possible order. Tuesday at 06:00Z the labour market report is expected to show unemployment RISING to 5.0% from 4.9%, average earnings including bonus FALLING to 3.9% from 4.1%, employment change +70K from +83K and a claimant count that TE forecasts at -5,000 against a +8,300 consensus. Wednesday at 06:00Z CPI is expected to RISE to 3.1% from 2.9% with core at 2.7%. Inflation accelerating into a loosening labour market is the configuration that freezes a committee, and the Bank of England decides Thursday at 11:00Z with TE carrying a 3.75% forecast and a 3/9 vote-hike consensus. Zero is not indecision here; it is the accurate reading of a distribution with mass on both sides. Seventh, the euro. EUR/USD closed the week at 1.15985 and is now 1.15535, down 0.39% today and 0.59% on the week, despite an ECB that hiked eleven days ago and told the market the Middle East conflict continues to fuel inflationary pressures. The euro is fully paid for its own central bank, and it now carries the largest energy-import bill on the board: German gas at 80.65 euros is up 29.32% on the month and EU gas at 82.94 is up 34.29%. That combination is why EUR/CAD moves from RANGE to SHORT today - the same barrel that helps Canada hurts the euro area - and why GER40 moves from RANGE to SHORT. Four ECB speakers are on the tape today alone: Schnabel at 09:15Z, Cipollone at 13:00Z, Lagarde at 15:15Z and Machado at 16:00Z, with euro-area Q2 wage growth at 3.4% due Wednesday. Any softening of the further-tightening language is the euro's main downside risk this week. Eighth, the kiwi remains the cleanest short leg. NZD/USD at 0.57823 was the worst major again today at -0.53%, is -1.61% on the week and -2.03% on the month, and it carries the HIGHEST headline inflation in the G10 at 4.1% with a central bank that has hiked twice. The RBNZ explained why itself: the Q2 spike was largely imported fuel, core and expectations remain consistent with a return to the 1-3% band by mid-2027, and the Committee flagged weak income growth, job insecurity and flat house prices. Consumer confidence at 80.4 from 94.7 is a fourteen-point collapse in a month. A central bank hiking into an energy shock it expects to fade earns a growth discount, not a currency bid. So the shape of the book today is unchanged at the score level and meaningfully changed at the symbol level: keep the yen crosses short and size them for Friday, keep USD/CHF and the CHF crosses long because two independent haven tests have now failed, re-pair USOIL LONG with CAD strength rather than against it, and move the copper-linked and energy-importing exposures - AUD/CAD, EUR/CAD, GER40, XCU - to the short side of the same supply shock.

USD.when: Sept 16, 18:00Z - TE carries consensus AND its own forecast at 4.00%, and CME FedWatch sits near 86%, up from 72% before last week's PPI
USD.note: TE re-verified this morning, unchanged: policy rate 3.75% upper bound, CPI 3.4% y/y with +0.4% m/m, unemployment 4.1%, non-farm payrolls +162,000, GDP +1.5% q/q and 2.1% annual, manufacturing PMI 53.9, services 56.5, retail sales -0.6% m/m, consumer confidence 47.8. USD holds at +2. The dollar index rose 0.32% to 99.439 today and beat every G10 except the Canadian dollar, which is a respectable session but not a trend - DXY is still only +0.27% on the week and -0.20% on the month despite an 86% hike probability. That gap between rate expectations and price is the whole USD story and it resolves Wednesday. The hike itself is bought. The Summary of Economic Projections is not: TE's projection rows still carry 3.6% for the first year and 3.4% for the second against 3.8% current, dots that imply EASING after this hike. Warsh has refused forward guidance since Jackson Hole on August 28, where he said the predominant focus should be on prices and that underlying inflation trends had not improved, so the dots are the only guidance on offer. The dovish hook inside the August CPI remains live - core on the ANNUAL rate slowed to 2.4%, the lowest since March 2021, with shelter at 3.0% and food at 2.7% while energy ran 16.3% - and a committee that wants to look through an oil shock has the data to do it. TD Securities reads the same print the other way and forecasts three hikes with the next two in October and January. Both are defensible, which is why conviction stays capped at +2. Retail sales Wednesday at 12:30Z, expected +0.9% m/m after -0.6%, is the last US data before the decision six hours later.

EUR.when: Late October - the ECB hiked on September 10 and the next monetary policy decision follows the September 30 non-policy meeting and the October 8 accounts, with nothing on TE's calendar before then
EUR.note: TE re-verified: deposit facility rate 2.50% (raised from 2.25% on September 10), main refinancing 2.65%, marginal lending 2.90%, HICP 3.3% y/y with +0.4% m/m, unemployment 6.4%, GDP +0.6% q/q and 1.2% annual, manufacturing PMI 52.7, services 51.6, balance of trade +8.6bn euros. The September 10 decision was the second hike since the war began; the ECB said the Middle East conflict continues to fuel inflationary pressures with inflation expected to stay well above 2% for an extended period, kept 2026 inflation at 3.0%, revised 2027 UP to 2.5% and 2028 UP to 2.1%, upgraded growth to 0.9% for 2026 and 1.4% for 2027, and Lagarde said growth risks are tilted to the downside while inflation risks are tilted to the UPSIDE. That is a hawkish package and the euro has already been paid for it: EUR/USD is 1.15535, down 0.39% today and 0.59% on the week. What is NOT yet in the price is the terms-of-trade cost. The euro area is the largest net energy importer on this board and German gas at 80.65 euros a megawatt-hour is up 29.32% on the month with EU gas at 82.94 up 34.29% - the same shock that supports the Canadian dollar taxes the euro. That is the basis for moving EUR/CAD to SHORT and GER40 to SHORT today. Four speakers on the tape today: Schnabel 09:15Z, Cipollone 13:00Z, Lagarde 15:15Z, Machado 16:00Z, with Buch and Schnabel again Tuesday. Euro-area Q2 wage growth at 3.4% lands Wednesday at 12:00Z and final August HICP Thursday at 09:00Z, expected to confirm 3.3% with core 2.4%. Any softening of the further-tightening language is the main downside risk.

JPY.when: Sept 18, 03:00Z - TE carries consensus AND its own forecast at 1.25%, with the September Reuters poll at 97% of 68 economists and market pricing near 80%
JPY.note: TE re-verified: policy rate 1.00%, CPI 1.9% y/y with +0.4% m/m, unemployment 2.4% and falling, GDP +0.4% q/q with 1.4% annualised and 0.7% annual, current account +2,989bn yen, manufacturing PMI 54.9, services 52.5, retail sales +2.4% m/m, business confidence 22 from 17. Today's session must be reported honestly: the yen LOST. USD/JPY rose 0.37% to 154.177 and the weekly decline has shrunk to -0.12% from -1.69% at Friday's close, though the monthly is still -3.31%. Yesterday JPY was held at +3 on the strength of a result - it beat the dollar on the hottest US core CPI day of the month - and that result did not repeat inside a broad dollar bid. The score holds at +3 because one 0.37% session is noise and because the forward case is intact and large: Friday's expected move to 1.25% is the highest policy rate since roughly September 1995, DBS calls the hike 'almost a done deal' with a hawkish 25bp the most likely outcome, 62% of surveyed economists see 1.75% by end-Q2 2027 and 89% see at least 1.50% by end-March. The Takaichi administration has been explicit about curbing excessive yen depreciation, and carry unwind plus repatriation are doing real work. But the description of the score changes today: it is a FORWARD call on Friday, not a validated result, and it should be sized that way. August CPI lands Thursday at 23:30Z with core expected near 1.8%, four hours before the decision. The single risk that cuts this score is a hike delivered with an explicit pause attached - that unwinds every SHORT XXX/JPY on the board simultaneously.

The rule is kept, so AUD holds +1, but this is now the weakest +1 on the board and the test has moved forward: China industrial production and retail sales print Tuesday at 05:00Z with consensus 4.8% and 0.8%. A miss on both, with copper already down 5% in five sessions, satisfies the trigger through the demand channel and AUD goes to zero. Hunter spoke today at 02:30Z. AUD/USD at 0.71404 is -0.38% today and -1.08% on the week but still +7.01% year-to-date, so the currency is unwinding a large gain rather than breaking.

NZD.note: TE re-verified: OCR 2.75% after the September 2 hike, CPI 4.1% y/y with +1.5% q/q, unemployment 5.6%, GDP +0.8% q/q and 1.5% annual, manufacturing PMI 53.1 from 54.3, consumer confidence 80.4 from 94.7, retail sales -0.5%, building permits 3,339 from 3,487, balance of trade -1,949m. This is still the currency that breaks the naive rule and it broke it again today. New Zealand has the HIGHEST headline inflation in the G10, its central bank has hiked twice in a row, and the kiwi was the worst major of the session at -0.53%, taking NZD/USD to 0.57823, -1.61% on the week and -2.03% on the month. The RBNZ's own statement is the explanation: the Q2 rise to 4.1% was largely fuel prices from the Middle East conflict, while core inflation, wage growth and expectations remain consistent with returning to the 1-3% band by mid-2027, and the Committee described weak income growth, job insecurity and flat house prices weighing on household spending and residential investment. Consumer confidence falling more than fourteen points in a single month is the market's read of that. A central bank raising rates into an energy shock it expects to fade earns a growth discount rather than a currency bid, and today's supply-shock escalation makes the fuel channel worse rather than better for a small, distant, energy-importing economy. TE's hold for October 28 confirms the pause. NZD stays at -1 and remains the cleanest short leg against the yen and against the dollar.

CAD.when: Late October - the BoC held on Sept 2 and its next decision follows the Oct 19 Business Outlook and Consumer Expectations surveys; the Summary of Deliberations is due Sept 16 at 17:30Z
CAD.note: TE re-verified: overnight rate 2.25%, CPI 3.0% y/y with +0.5% m/m, unemployment 6.4%, GDP +0.8% q/q with 3.3% annualised and 1.1% annual, employment -41,700, retail sales -0.8% m/m, manufacturing PMI 53.0, business confidence 64.3 from 55.1, current account +8.8bn. Today is the day the petro-currency channel started transmitting again, and the reason is the character of the oil move rather than its size. Last week Brent gained 9% on a risk premium and USD/CAD ROSE 0.25%. Today Brent gained 2.09% because Saudi Arabia's main Hormuz-bypass pipeline is physically shut with five to seven days of Yanbu cover, and USD/CAD was flat at 1.38770 - the best G10 result of a session in which the dollar index rose 0.32% and beat everything else. Risk premia do not move the terms of trade; supply shocks do. That reverses yesterday's explicit statement that USOIL LONG and CAD LONG were no longer the same trade, and it is today's main symbol-level change. CAD is NOT upgraded to +2, on discipline: August CPI prints at 12:30Z today with headline consensus 3.0% y/y, the MONTHLY rate expected to fall to 0.0% from +0.5%, core 2.3% y/y, trimmed-mean 1.9%, median 2.0% and CPI common 2.7%. Core measures at or below target keep the Bank frozen no matter where crude trades, and the domestic picture is genuinely soft with 41,700 jobs lost in August and retail sales -0.8%. Raising a score hours before its own inflation print, on one session, is the noise-chasing this file avoids. If today's CPI lands at or above consensus, CAD is the first upgrade candidate on the board. Wednesday's Summary of Deliberations at 17:30Z shows whether the internal split is moving ahead of the data.

CHF.when: Sept 24, 07:30Z - TE carries a 0% consensus and a 0% forecast
CHF.note: TE re-verified: SNB policy rate 0.00%, CPI 0.8% y/y with +0.4% m/m, unemployment 3.0%, GDP +1.5% q/q and 2.3% annual, manufacturing PMI 57.1 from 53.2, business confidence 107 from 104, current account 7.1% of GDP. Yesterday CHF was cut from +1 to zero on the argument that a haven refusing to bid on a burning tanker cannot be held long. That call is validated today by a second, completely independent test. The Hormuz bypass pipeline stayed shut, Gulf-Iran diplomacy was postponed with no new date, and GOLD - which has no central bank, no intervention risk and no policy rate attached to it - FELL 0.50% to 4328.57 while silver fell 0.67%. Two unrelated havens refused the same escalation on the same day. USD/CHF rose another 0.26% to 0.81862 and is now +1.12% on the week, +0.96% on the month and +3.25% year-to-date. The June SNB statement is the frame that still applies: rate held at 0%, medium-term inflation pressures largely unchanged despite energy-driven increases, annual average inflation forecast at 0.6% for 2026 and 2027 and 0.7% for 2028, growth of 1.0% and 1.5%, Middle East tensions named as a risk that could STRENGTHEN the franc, and a signalled greater readiness to intervene in FX. That last clause now cuts one way only, because the franc is not strengthening on the tension the SNB warned about. September 24 is a certain hold; the only readable content is whether the intervention language is repeated, and with the franc failing to bid it almost certainly is, which is itself bearish. CHF stays at zero and the CHF crosses stay long.

Yesterday JPY was held at +3 because it beat the dollar on the hottest US data day of the month - a result. Today that result did not repeat: the yen lost 0.37% inside a broad dollar bid. One session is noise and the forward case is large and intact - Friday's move to 1.25% is a 31-year high, DBS calls it 'almost a done deal' with a hawkish 25bp most likely, 62% of surveyed economists see 1.75% by end-Q2 2027 and 89% see at least 1.50% by end-March, and the Takaichi administration is openly hostile to further yen depreciation. But the honest label is that +3 is now a FORWARD bet on Friday rather than a validated trend, and it should be sized as one. What would invalidate it: a hike delivered Thursday-Friday with an explicit pause attached, or a soft August core CPI at 23:30Z Thursday that lets the board frame 1.25% as terminal. That single outcome unwinds every SHORT XXX/JPY on this board simultaneously, which is why conviction on USD/JPY and CAD/JPY is cut to MEDIUM today.

The reason is that the euro area is the largest net energy importer on this board and the same supply shock that lifts Brent taxes European industry directly: EU gas 82.94 euros up 34.29% on the month, German gas 80.65 up 29.32%. Policy tightening is priced; the terms-of-trade drag is not. That asymmetry is the basis for today's two changes - EUR/CAD from RANGE to SHORT and GER40 from RANGE to SHORT. What would invalidate the +1 downward: any of today's four speakers (Schnabel 09:15Z, Cipollone 13:00Z, Lagarde 15:15Z, Machado 16:00Z) softening the further-tightening language, or Wednesday's Q2 wage growth undershooting 3.4%. catalysts.event: Strait of Hormuz and Iran-US escalation
catalysts.note: Oman postponed Monday's Gulf-Iran meeting 'in the interests of consensus' with no new date, hours after a vessel was struck near Qeshm Island killing one and injuring four. Trump said Iran is 'calling constantly' but declined to say whether the US struck the ship. Hormuz traffic remains roughly 90% below pre-war levels. Watch for a rescheduled Muscat date - that is the de-escalation trigger that reverses the oil complex.

catalysts.event: Yen intervention and BoJ pace watch
catalysts.note: USD/JPY is 154.177, -3.31% on the month but only -0.12% on the week after today's 0.37% rise. Official yen buying earlier this month lowered the political barrier to BoJ hikes rather than substituting for them, and the Takaichi administration remains openly opposed to further depreciation.

geopolitics: Two doors closed over the weekend and the market repriced only one channel. First, Saudi Arabia's East-West Crude Oil Pipeline - Petroline, 1,200 kilometres from the Eastern Province to the Red Sea port of Yanbu, carrying roughly 5 million barrels a day of crude that would otherwise transit the Gulf - was struck by drones launched from Iraqi territory on September 10 and 11 and remains shut as a precaution. Riyadh issued its strongest condemnation but said it would not retaliate for now, at Baghdad's request. Traders told Reuters that stored volumes at Yanbu cover exports for only five to seven days; past that window as much as 4% of global supply is exposed. This matters more than another tanker strike because Petroline IS the bypass - the physical answer to a closed Hormuz - and with it offline there is no workaround left. Second, late on September 13 Omani Foreign Minister Badr Albusaidi announced that Monday's Gulf Cooperation Council-Iran meeting on the Hormuz shipping proposal had been postponed 'in the interests of consensus', at the request of unnamed regional states and by joint Tehran-Muscat decision, with no new date set. The postponement came hours after an attack near Qeshm Island, about 22km from Bandar Abbas, killed one and wounded four aboard an Iranian commercial vessel; UKMTO separately reported a vessel hit by a projectile with a severe fire and evacuation. Iran's president said 'Iran won't surrender'; Trump said Iran 'wants to make a deal so bad' that they are 'calling constantly', and when asked whether the US struck the vessel replied 'I don't want to say'. The underlying dispute is unchanged: Muscat's July proposal to split control of the strait 50-50 with voluntary transit fees was rejected by Tehran, which insists fees be compulsory and that it will not reopen the strait until the US naval blockade of Iranian ports is lifted. Hormuz traffic remains roughly 90% below pre-war levels against about 20 million barrels a day before February 28. Trump is pushing to restore flows ahead of November's midterms, which is the strongest force for de-escalation on the board and also the reason a sudden deal headline is a live tail risk. The FX transmission is unusually clean and unusually narrow. Energy repriced: WTI +2.17% to 102.226, Brent +2.09% to 106.795, EU gas +4.30% to 82.94 euros with the monthly at +34.29%, German gas 80.65 at +29.32% monthly, gasoline +1.61%. Havens did not: gold FELL 0.50% to 4328.57, silver fell 0.67% to 63.834, and USD/CHF ROSE 0.26% to 0.81862. That divergence is the single most important read on this page - the war is being expressed exclusively through physical energy, while US real rates own the haven bid. It is also why the demand-side counterweight matters: the IEA cut its 2026 global demand forecast to a DECLINE of 2.5 million barrels a day from 1.6 million in August, OPEC cut its demand-growth forecast for a fifth consecutive month and the EIA still projects Brent averaging near $90 in H2 on a gradual Hormuz recovery. Crude is rising on supply despite a deteriorating demand picture, which makes the rally fragile to exactly one headline: a pipeline restart or a rescheduled Muscat date. Practically: hold USOIL LONG and pair it WITH CAD strength rather than against it, since the terms-of-trade channel is transmitting again; keep the CHF crosses long because two structurally unrelated havens have now refused the same escalation; short the energy importers of this shock through EUR/CAD, GER40 and the NZD crosses; and keep XAU and XAG short as a Fed trade rather than a war trade, with Wednesday's dot plot - not the Strait - as the event that decides them.
